summary30s: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915; his mentor Gopal Krishna Gokhale advised him to tour the country for a year before engaging in politics.
His first major public appearance was at the opening of Banaras Hindu University (BHU) in February 1916, where he admonished the elite for ignoring the millions of poor peasants.
Early localized satyagrahas in Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad (1918), and Kheda (1918) established his grassroots technique of non-violent mass struggle.
The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) united with Khilafat; called off after the violent Chauri Chaura incident in February 1922.
The Salt March (12 March - 6 April 1930) mobilized women and masses against the British salt monopoly, leading to the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and the 1942 Quit India Movement ('Do or Die').

coreConcepts.title: Return to India and Early Satyagrahas (1915-1918)
coreConcepts.explanation: Gandhiji returned to India in January 1915 after 20 years in South Africa, where he had forged the weapon of Satyagraha. On the advice of Gopal Krishna Gokhale, he spent his first year travelling across the country. In February 1916, he spoke at the opening of Banaras Hindu University (BHU), famously declaring: 'There is no salvation for India unless you strip yourselves of this jewellery and hold it in trust for your countrymen in India.' In 1917, at the request of Rajkumar Shukla, he intervened in Champaran (Bihar) against the oppressive European indigo planters (tinkathia system). In 1918, he led a strike of textile mill workers in Ahmedabad demanding a 35% wage increase, followed by the Kheda Satyagraha supporting peasants facing crop failure.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part III, Section 1
coreConcepts.examTip: Chronology of early satyagrahas: Champaran (1917) -> Ahmedabad Mill Strike (early 1918) -> Kheda (mid 1918).

coreConcepts.title: Rowlatt Satyagraha and Non-Cooperation Movement (1919-1922)
coreConcepts.explanation: In 1919, the British passed the Rowlatt Act, allowing detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhi called for a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919. On 13 April 1919, General Dyer ordered troops to fire upon an unarmed gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. In 1920, Gandhi linked Non-Cooperation with the Khilafat Movement led by Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali to forge Hindu-Muslim unity. The movement entailed boycotting government schools, law courts, foreign cloth, and surrendering titles. On 4 February 1922, a crowd attacked and set fire to a police station at Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur, UP), killing 22 policemen. Committed strictly to Ahimsa, Gandhi immediately called off the Non-Cooperation Movement.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part III, Section 2
coreConcepts.examTip: Chauri Chaura occurred in February 1922 in Gorakhpur district, prompting Gandhi to suspend Non-Cooperation unconditionally.

coreConcepts.title: The Salt March and Civil Disobedience (1930-1931)
coreConcepts.explanation: At the Lahore Congress of December 1929, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, the goal of 'Purna Swaraj' (complete independence) was proclaimed, and 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day. Gandhi launched Civil Disobedience against the state salt monopoly. On 12 March 1930, Gandhi marched from his Sabarmati Ashram with 78 chosen volunteers, covering 240 miles in 24 days to reach Dandi on 5 April. On morning of 6 April 1930, he picked up a handful of natural salt, breaking the colonial salt law. The march made Gandhi world-famous (covered widely by Time magazine) and saw massive participation by women (urged by socialist Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay). In March 1931, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed: British agreed to release political prisoners not guilty of violence and permit coastal salt-making, while Congress suspended Civil Disobedience and agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part III, Sections 3 & 4
coreConcepts.examTip: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay persuaded Gandhi not to restrict the salt protests to men, inaugurating mass female political mobilization.

coreConcepts.title: Quit India (1942), Cabinet Mission, and Partition
coreConcepts.explanation: Following the failure of the Cripps Mission in March 1942, Gandhi launched the 'Quit India Movement' from Bombay on 8 August 1942, issuing the historic mantra: 'Do or Die' (Karo ya Maro). The British arrested the entire Congress Working Committee on 9 August. Mass spontaneous uprisings followed: parallel governments ('Prati Sarkar') were established in Satara (Maharashtra) and Midnapore (Jatiya Sarkar). Underground networks were run by Jayaprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali, and Ram Manohar Lohia. In 1946, the British sent the Cabinet Mission (Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, A.V. Alexander) proposing a three-tiered confederation, but it collapsed over grouping clauses. On 16 August 1946, the Muslim League launched 'Direct Action Day', triggering deadly communal violence in Calcutta. Lord Mountbatten announced the partition plan on 3 June 1947, and on 15 August 1947, India gained independence.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part III, Section 5
coreConcepts.examTip: Three members of 1946 Cabinet Mission: Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander.

workedExamples.question:
Which socialist leader persuaded Mahatma Gandhi not to restrict the Salt Satyagraha protests solely to men, leading to thousands of women courting arrest?
(A) Sarojini Naidu
(B) Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay
(C) Aruna Asaf Ali
(D) Sucheta Kripalani
workedExamples.explanation: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay, a socialist activist, persuaded Gandhiji not to restrict the protests to men. Kamaladevi herself was among numerous women who courted arrest by breaking the salt and liquor laws.
solutionStepByStep: Step 1: Check NCERT Theme 11 Section 3: 'The Salt Satyagraha: A Case Study'.
Step 2: Explicitly names Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay as the activist who convinced Gandhi to open the movement to women.
workedExamples.cuetPattern: Women's agency and historical interventions in the freedom struggle.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Check NCERT Theme 11 Section 3: 'The Salt Satyagraha: A Case Study'.
Step 2: Explicitly names Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay as the activist who convinced Gandhi to open the movement to women.

workedExamples.question:
Arrange the following historical events in chronological order:
(i) Chauri Chaura incident
(ii) Champaran Satyagraha
(iii) Gandhi-Irwin Pact
(iv) Launch of Quit India Movement
workedExamples.explanation: Champaran Satyagraha took place in 1917; Chauri Chaura incident occurred in February 1922; Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed in March 1931; Quit India Movement was launched on 8 August 1942.
solutionStepByStep: Conclusion: Sequence is (ii), (i), (iii), (iv). Option A is correct.
workedExamples.cuetPattern: Standard chronological sequence question on modern Indian history.
solutionSteps: Conclusion: Sequence is (ii), (i), (iii), (iv). Option A is correct.

commonTraps.misconception: Assuming Gandhi attended all three Round Table Conferences in London.
commonTraps.correctConcept: Congress boycotted the First (1930) and Third (1932) Round Table Conferences. Gandhi attended ONLY the Second Round Table Conference (autumn 1931) as the sole representative of the Congress.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Questions ask 'Which Round Table Conference(s) did Gandhi attend?' and students pick 'All three' or 'First and Second'.
commonTraps.cuetWarning: Gandhi attended ONLY the Second Round Table Conference (1931).

commonTraps.misconception: Believing the Lahore Session of Congress happened in 1930.
commonTraps.correctConcept: The historic Lahore Congress Session occurred in DECEMBER 1929 under Jawaharlal Nehru, where Purna Swaraj was adopted; 26 January 1930 was chosen as Independence Day.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: 26 January 1930 leads students to misdate the session itself to 1930.
commonTraps.cuetWarning: Session = December 1929; Independence Day celebration = 26 January 1930.

practiceQuestions.question: Whom did Mahatma Gandhi acknowledge as his political mentor upon returning to India in 1915?
practiceQuestions.explanation: On Gokhale's advice, Gandhiji spent a year travelling around British India, getting to know the land and its peoples.

practiceQuestions.question: In which year did the violent incident at Chauri Chaura take place, prompting Gandhi to call off the Non-Cooperation Movement?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In February 1922, a crowd of peasants attacked and burnt a police station in Chauri Chaura, prompting Gandhi to call off the movement.

practiceQuestions.question: How many chosen volunteers accompanied Mahatma Gandhi when he set out on the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi walked with 78 volunteers from his ashram at Sabarmati to the Gujarati coastal village of Dandi.

practiceQuestions.question: At which historic Congress session was the resolution of 'Purna Swaraj' (Complete Independence) formally adopted under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru?
practiceQuestions.explanation: At the end of December 1929, the Congress held its annual session in Lahore. The meeting was significant for the election of Jawaharlal Nehru as President, and the proclamation of commitment to Purna Swaraj.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the three Round Table Conferences held in London was attended by Mahatma Gandhi as the sole representative of the Indian National Congress?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A Second Round Table Conference was held in London in late 1931. Here, Gandhiji represented the Congress as its sole representative.

practiceQuestions.question: What historic mantra did Mahatma Gandhi give to the nation on launching the Quit India Movement in August 1942?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Addressing the Congress delegates at Gowalia Tank in Bombay, Gandhi gave the call 'Do or Die'.

practiceQuestions.question: During the Quit India Movement of 1942, an independent parallel government called 'Prati Sarkar' was established in which district of Maharashtra?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In Satara (Maharashtra), a parallel government called the 'Prati Sarkar' was set up under leaders like Nana Patil.

practiceQuestions.question: Who was the peasant cultivator from Champaran who persistently met Gandhiji at Lucknow and Kanpur to persuade him to visit Champaran?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rajkumar Shukla, an agriculturist from Champaran, met Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress in December 1916 and persuaded him to visit.

practiceQuestions.question: Which American news magazine initially derided Mahatma Gandhi's physical appearance during the Salt March, but later lauded him as a 'Saint' after the movement's success?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Time magazine initially scoffed at Gandhi's spindly frame, but within weeks changed its tune, saluting him as a Saint and Statesman.

practiceQuestions.question:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Mahatma Gandhi chose common salt as the central symbol of the 1930 Civil Disobedience movement.
Reason (R): Salt was an indispensable commodity consumed equally by every household, and the British state monopoly and tax on salt was a universally felt grievance uniting all Indians across caste and religion.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

practiceQuestions.explanation: Gandhi recognized salt as a universal necessity. The tax fell heavily on the poorest, making it an ideal symbol to unite the nation. Both are true and (R) explains (A).
